abstract: |
  Full random-effects modelling (FREM) jointly describes individual parameters
  and covariates using a multivariate Normal population distribution. We extend
  FREM by combining Gaussian dependence with prespecified continuous marginal
  distributions for parameter random effects and continuous or ordered
  categorical marginal distributions for covariates. The model reduces to
  Gaussian FREM when all margins are Normal and permits missing covariates.
  We derive the observed-data likelihood and estimate population locations,
  marginal-distribution parameters, dependence parameters and residual error
  jointly by controlled-MCMC stochastic approximation. The fitted conditional
  model has an exact conventional FFEM representation when parameter margins
  are Normal and an exact conditional generative representation otherwise.
  In 400 simulated nonlinear mixed-effects datasets, structural-parameter bias
  remained within 0.47%. Relative to Gaussian FREM, mean differences in
  observed log likelihood were 4.30--9.41 under non-Gaussian data-generating
  distributions and -0.06 under a Gaussian data-generating distribution. Among
  subjects above the 95th percentile of a Gamma-distributed covariate, flexible
  margins reduced the log-scale RMSE of VPC quantiles by 54%. These results
  indicate that marginal-distribution
  assumptions can materially affect conditional prediction while Gaussian
  FREM remains available as a special case.

**Keywords:** nonlinear mixed-effects model; full random-effects model;
Gaussian copula; stochastic approximation; marginal likelihood; covariates

# INTRODUCTION

Covariate models describe how patient characteristics contribute to variability
in individual model parameters and predictions. Full random-effects modelling
(FREM) includes a prespecified set of covariates as additional random effects
and estimates their joint covariance with the parameter random effects
[@yngman2022]. Covariate-effect coefficients and unexplained parameter
variability can then be calculated for any subset of the included covariates
from a single estimation. This avoids repeated estimation of separate reduced
covariate models and allows missing covariates to be integrated over in the
likelihood [@nyberg2024; @jonsson2024].

Standard FREM assumes that the combined parameter and covariate random effects
are multivariate Normal. For covariates observed with negligible error, this
working model can estimate means and covariances accurately under some
non-Normal covariate distributions [@yngman2022]. It nevertheless specifies the
entire population distribution, including marginal shape and conditional tail
behaviour. These features are relevant when the fitted model is used for
conditional prediction, simulation of virtual populations, integration over
missing covariates, or extrapolation to sparsely represented covariate values.

A copula permits the marginal distributions to be specified separately from
their dependence [@sklar1959; @joe1996]. We extend FREM by combining a Gaussian
copula with prespecified continuous margins for parameter random effects and
continuous or ordered categorical margins for covariates. The multivariate
Normal FREM model is recovered when all margins are Normal. Estimation is based
on the joint observed-data likelihood of the responses and recorded covariates,
with individual parameters and missing covariates treated as unobserved data.

The objectives of this work were to define the flexible-margin FREM model,
derive its observed-data likelihood and an exact FFEM translation, develop a
likelihood-based stochastic-approximation estimator, and evaluate parameter
recovery and conditional prediction in a simulation study.

# METHODS

## FREM model

For subject $i$ at design point $x_{ij}$, the nonlinear mixed-effects
observation model is

\[
 y_{ij}=f(\psi_i,x_{ij})+g(\psi_i,\sigma,x_{ij})\epsilon_{ij},
 \qquad \epsilon_{ij}\sim N(0,1),                          \tag{1}
\]

where $\psi_i$ is the vector of individual model parameters and $\sigma$
contains the residual-error parameters. On the transformed additive scale,

\[
 \phi_i=h(\psi_i)=C_i\mu+\eta_{\mathrm{par},i},             \tag{2}
\]

where $C_i$ is the fixed-effect design matrix, $\mu$ is the vector of
population parameters, and $\eta_{\mathrm{par},i}$ is the parameter random
effect. The lowercase symbol $c_i$ denotes the FREM covariate vector and
distinguishes it from the design matrix $C_i$. An error-free additive FREM
covariate model is

\[
 c_i=\mu_c+\eta_{\mathrm{cov},i}.                           \tag{3}
\]

Here $\eta_{\mathrm{par},i}$ represents total parameter variability (TPV) and
$\eta_{\mathrm{cov},i}$ is the individual covariate deviation. Standard FREM
specifies

\[
 \begin{pmatrix}\eta_{\mathrm{par},i}\\
                 \eta_{\mathrm{cov},i}\end{pmatrix}
 \sim N\!\left[0,\Omega_{\mathrm{FREM}}\right],\qquad
 \Omega_{\mathrm{FREM}}=
 \begin{pmatrix}
  \Omega_{\mathrm{par}}&\Omega_{\mathrm{par,cov}}\\
  \Omega_{\mathrm{cov,par}}&\Omega_{\mathrm{cov}}
 \end{pmatrix}.                                             \tag{4}
\]

Equation (4) is the standard FREM specification [@yngman2022]. Let
$\Omega_{\mathrm{par,cov}}\in\R^{p\times q}$ and
$\Omega_{\mathrm{cov,par}}=\Omega_{\mathrm{par,cov}}^{\mathsf T}$.
The covariate-effect matrix and unexplained parameter variability (UPV) are

\[
 B=\Omega_{\mathrm{par,cov}}\Omega_{\mathrm{cov}}^{-1},
 \qquad
 \Omega'_{\mathrm{par}}
 =\Omega_{\mathrm{par}}-B\Omega_{\mathrm{cov,par}}.        \tag{5}
\]

Consequently,

\[
 \eta_{\mathrm{par},i}\mid c_i
 \sim N\!\left[B(c_i-\mu_c),
                  \Omega'_{\mathrm{par}}\right].           \tag{6}
\]

Equations (4)--(6) give the standard Gaussian FREM model, its conditional
covariate coefficients, and its UPV representation.

## Flexible-margin FREM model

Let $X_i=(\eta_{\mathrm{par},i},c_i)$ contain the $d$ population coordinates.
For continuous coordinate $j$, write $F_j(\cdot;\alpha_j)$ and
$f_j(\cdot;\alpha_j)$ for its CDF and density and define

\[
 \xi_j=\Phi^{-1}\{F_j(x_j;\alpha_j)\}.
\]

Let $R(\rho)$ be a positive-definite Gaussian-score correlation matrix and let
$\theta_p=(\alpha,\rho)$ collect the population-distribution parameters. The
continuous population density is

\[
 p_{\theta_p}(x)=|R|^{-1/2}
 \exp\!\left[-\tfrac12\xi^{\mathsf T}(R^{-1}-I)\xi\right]
 \prod_{j=1}^d f_j(x_j;\alpha_j).                           \tag{7}
\]

We parameterize $R$ by a fixed regular vine with Gaussian pair copulas; the vine
structure is not estimated during the stochastic-approximation recursion. When
all margins are Normal on their modelled scales, (7) reduces
exactly to the error-free Gaussian FREM population model (2)--(4), with
$\Omega_{\mathrm{FREM}}$ obtained from the marginal standard deviations and
$R$. This error-free formulation is the zero-covariate-residual limit of the
conventional NONMEM/PsN formulation, which uses a small fixed residual variance for covariate
responses [@yngman2022; @jonsson2024].

Let $\theta=(\mu,\alpha,\rho,\sigma)$ denote the unknown parameter vector.
Here $\alpha$ contains the parameters of the marginal distributions of
$\eta_{\mathrm{par}}$ and $c$, including $\mu_c$; $\rho$ parameterizes $R$; and $\sigma$
contains the residual-error parameters. When all margins are Normal,
the marginal scale parameters together with $\rho$ are equivalently represented
by $\operatorname{vec}(\Omega_{\mathrm{FREM}})$; the covariate locations
$\mu_c$ remain separate.

The corresponding FREM effect summaries live naturally on the latent-score
scale. Partition $R$ into individual-parameter and covariate blocks. Then

\[
 B_\xi=R_{\mathrm{par,cov}}R_{\mathrm{cov}}^{-1},\qquad
 R'_{\mathrm{par}}=R_{\mathrm{par}}-
 B_\xi R_{\mathrm{cov,par}},                              \tag{7a}
\]

so that $\xi_{\mathrm{par}}\mid c$ is Normal with mean
$B_\xi\xi_{\mathrm{cov}}(c)$ and covariance $R'_{\mathrm{par}}$. The fitted
marginal quantile maps transform this conditional law back to the native
parameter scale. Under all-Normal margins, let $D_{\mathrm{par}}$ and
$D_{\mathrm{cov}}$ be diagonal matrices of marginal standard deviations. Then
$B=D_{\mathrm{par}}B_\xi D_{\mathrm{cov}}^{-1}$ and
$\Omega'_{\mathrm{par}}=D_{\mathrm{par}}R'_{\mathrm{par}}
D_{\mathrm{par}}$, which recovers (5). Under non-Gaussian parameter margins the
native-scale conditional mean need not be linear. In that case, $B_\xi$,
$R'_{\mathrm{par}}$ and the marginal quantile functions jointly determine the
conditional distribution.

## Maximum likelihood estimation

For the Gaussian FREM model, the complete-data likelihood has the curved
exponential-family representation used by standard SAEM,

\[
 \log p_\theta(Y,Z)=-\psi(\theta)+
 \langle S(Y,Z),\varphi(\theta)\rangle,
\]

where $S(Y,Z)$ is a parameter-independent finite-dimensional sufficient
statistic. Standard SAEM recursively averages $S(Y,Z)$ and performs the M-step
from that finite vector [@delyon1999; @kuhn2005].

In (7), a marginal parameter $\alpha_j$ enters both
$\log f_j(x_j;\alpha_j)$ and the transformed value
$\xi_j=\Phi^{-1}\{F_j(x_j;\alpha_j)\}$ inside the copula quadratic form.
Marginal and dependence parameters are therefore coupled through nonlinear
functions of the latent data, and a parameter-independent finite statistic
$S(Y,Z)$ is not generally available. The observed-data likelihood and the EM
identity remain valid, but the usual finite-statistic SAEM recursion and its
convergence theorem cannot simply be carried over. The likelihood score instead
provides a stochastic-approximation target through Delyon et al. equation (74).
When all margins are Normal, the ordinary Gaussian FREM finite-statistic
representation is recovered.

### Observed-data likelihood

Let $O_i=(Y_i,c_{i,\mathrm{obs}})$ and let $Z_i$ collect individual parameters
and missing covariates. For categorical covariates and continuous margins with
parameter-dependent support, $Z_i$ additionally contains the fixed-support
unit-interval variables defined below. With a fixed mixed Lebesgue/counting
measure $\lambda$, define the complete-data likelihood $f_i$ and observed-data
likelihood $g_i$ by

\[
 g_i(\theta)=\int f_i(z_i;\theta)\,\lambda(dz_i),\qquad
 \ell(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^N\log g_i(\theta).                 \tag{8}
\]

The dependence of $f_i$ and $g_i$ on $O_i$ is implicit, as in Delyon et al.;
$Z_i$ denotes the missing or augmented data [@delyon1999]. Consequently, the
likelihood contribution is based on the joint density
$p_\theta(Y_i,c_{i,\mathrm{obs}})$. Individual effects and missing covariates
are integrated out rather than replaced by point estimates. The analysis
conditions on the recorded missingness pattern and assumes that the
covariate-missingness mechanism is ignorable.

When all covariates are observed, its subject contribution has the exact
factorization

\[
 \log p_\theta(Y_i,c_i)
 =\log p_{\theta_p}(c_i)
  +\log p_\theta(Y_i\mid c_i).                             \tag{8a}
\]

Thus a difference in joint log likelihood may reflect differences in the
fitted covariate density, the conditional response likelihood, or both. This
factorization does not alter the estimation objective in (8).

When the continuous margins are proper and absolutely continuous, the required
fixed-support representations exist, the categorical probability vectors are
proper, $R$ is positive definite, and the response density is proper, (7)
defines a probability distribution and $g_i(\theta)$ in (8) is a valid
observed-data likelihood contribution. This follows from a componentwise
probability-integral transformation: continuous Jacobians transform (7) to a
$N_d(0,R)$ density, categorical cells partition their latent Gaussian
coordinates, and the fixed-support representations put moving boundaries on
fixed unit intervals. Appendix A gives the detailed normalization argument.

### Stochastic approximation of the likelihood score

Work in unconstrained internal coordinates $\vartheta$, with native parameters
$\theta=\tau(\vartheta)$. Log, logit and hyperspherical transformations enforce
positive scales, probabilities and a positive-definite $R$. Write
$\widetilde f_i(z;\vartheta)=f_i\{z;\tau(\vartheta)\}$ and
$\widetilde g_i(\vartheta)=g_i\{\tau(\vartheta)\}$. At iteration $k$,
controlled Markov kernels invariant for the current individual conditional law
advance $m$ chains per subject. The estimated complete score is

\[
 \widehat H_{k+1}=\frac1{mN}\sum_{r=1}^m\sum_{i=1}^N
 \nabla_\vartheta\log f_i
       (Z_{i,k+1}^{(r)};\tau(\vartheta_k)),                  \tag{9}
\]

and the parameter update is

\[
 \vartheta_{k+1}=\operatorname{Proj}_K
 \{\vartheta_k+\gamma_{k+1}A_k\widehat H_{k+1}\}.         \tag{10}
\]

Adaptation of the positive diagonal metric and proposal scales is restricted to
a finite initial sequence; these quantities are subsequently held fixed. The
gain sequence is
$\gamma_k=\gamma_0(k+k_0)^{-a}$ with $a>3/4$. Marginal families, category
order, copula structure and all other discrete model choices are specified
before recursion (10) begins.

Equation (10) is the internal-coordinate, projected, preconditioned and
multiple-chain extension of Delyon et al. equation (74),
$\theta_k=\theta_{k-1}+\gamma_k\partial_\theta
\log f(Z_k;\theta_{k-1})$. The coordinate transformations and fixed
positive-definite metric leave the stationary points unchanged.

Every stochastic move is either an exact conditional draw or a Metropolis-
Hastings transition with the current individual conditional law as invariant
distribution. At least one exact conditional-population independence proposal
is used per iteration. With several categorical covariates, random-walk moves
that would require a numerical rectangle probability are omitted; the exact
independence kernel remains. An unadjusted approximate kernel would generally
have a different invariant distribution and hence a different mean field
[@gruffaz2024].

### Relation to the observed-data likelihood

Provided differentiation can pass through (8), Fisher's identity gives

\[
 E_\vartheta\{\nabla_\vartheta\log \widetilde f_i(Z_i;\vartheta)\mid O_i\}
 =\nabla_\vartheta\log \widetilde g_i(\vartheta).           \tag{11}
\]

For one subject, substitution of the conditional density
$\widetilde f_i(z;\vartheta)/\widetilde g_i(\vartheta)$ into the expectation
reduces its numerator to
$\nabla_\vartheta\int \widetilde f_i(z;\vartheta)\lambda(dz)$.
The fixed-support representations ensure that $\lambda$ is fixed. Appendix A states the required
domination conditions and gives the full calculation [@louis1982].

Let $\bar\ell=N^{-1}\ell$. Thus the mean field after finite tuning is
$A\nabla\bar\ell$. For symmetric positive-definite $A$,

\[
 \frac{d}{dt}\bar\ell\{\vartheta(t)\}
 =\nabla\bar\ell(\vartheta)^{\mathsf T}A
  \nabla\bar\ell(\vartheta)\geq0.                          \tag{12}
\]

### Convergence

Let $\mathcal L=\{\vartheta:\nabla\bar\ell(\vartheta)=0\}$. Assume:

1. the model, augmentation and dominating measure are fixed, and
   $\bar\ell$ is continuously differentiable on a neighbourhood of the visited
   compact interior set;
2. differentiation under the integral is dominated, category probabilities
   and eigenvalues of $R$ stay away from zero, and moving-support quantile and
   response paths have dominated derivatives;
3. the controlled kernels have unique invariant laws, uniform geometric drift
   and minorization on the visited compact set, and the kernel and score satisfy
   the local regularity and Poisson-equation bounds required for Markovian
   stochastic approximation;
4. $\gamma_k=\gamma_0(k+k_0)^{-a}$ satisfies the usual summability conditions and the
   stronger controlled-Markov requirement; the value $a=0.80$ used in the
   experiments is valid for the stated Lipschitz and second-moment setting;
5. the metric is eventually fixed and positive definite, numerical score error
   is gain-weighted summable, and projections, invalid-step backtracking and
   no-move replacements cease after a finite random time; and
6. $-\bar\ell$ admits the required coercive Lyapunov extension and critical-
   value condition on the stabilized tail.

Then controlled-Markov stochastic-approximation results imply

\[
 d(\vartheta_k,\mathcal L)\longrightarrow0
 \qquad\text{almost surely}.                               \tag{13}
\]

The limit set lies in a connected component of $\mathcal L$. If it is contained
in a neighbourhood with one isolated attracting stationary point, the raw
iterates converge to that point. This result establishes convergence to the
stationary set, not convergence to a global maximum. It is distinct from
Delyon et al. Theorems 5 and 8, which concern finite-statistic SAEM. Appendix B
maps the assumptions to controlled-Markov results [@andrieu2005; @fort2016].

## Conditional representation and FFEM translation

For a selected covariate subset $S$, let $z_{iS}$ contain the corresponding
Gaussian scores and calculate $B_{\xi,S}$ and
$R'_{\mathrm{par},S}$ from the relevant blocks of $R$. If the parameter random-
effect margins are Normal, the fitted conditional distribution has the exact
FFEM representation

\[
 \phi_i=C_i\mu+\beta_{z,S}z_{iS}+\eta'_{iS},\qquad
 \beta_{z,S}=D_{\mathrm{par}}B_{\xi,S},\qquad
 \eta'_{iS}\sim N(0,\Omega'_{\mathrm{par},S}),
\]

where
$\Omega'_{\mathrm{par},S}=D_{\mathrm{par}}R'_{\mathrm{par},S}
D_{\mathrm{par}}$. The covariates are fixed inputs in this FFEM; their fitted
CDFs are used only to calculate $z_{iS}$. If the selected covariate margins are
also Normal, the transformation reduces to centring and scaling, and the usual
raw-scale $B_S$ and $\Omega'_{\mathrm{par},S}$ of standard FREM are recovered
[@yngman2022].

For non-Normal parameter random effects, a conventional additive-Normal FFEM
is not generally equivalent. Let $Q_\eta$ apply the fitted parameter-margin
quantile functions componentwise and choose $L_S$ such that
$L_SL_S^{\mathsf T}=R'_{\mathrm{par},S}$. The exact conditional representation
is

\[
 \phi_i=C_i\mu+
 Q_\eta\!\left[\Phi\!\left\{
 B_{\xi,S}z_{iS}+L_S\varepsilon_i\right\}\right],
 \qquad \varepsilon_i\sim N(0,I).
\]

The covariates remain fixed inputs, but the latent Normal random effects are
transformed to retain the fitted non-Normal parameter margins. We use
*distributional FFEM* as shorthand for this exact conditional generative
representation, not for a conventional additive-Normal FFEM. Ordered
categorical covariates similarly require their latent-interval mixture rather
than one deterministic transformed value. The implementation
exports the linear coefficient and UPV matrices when the conventional FFEM is
exact; otherwise the fitted conditional model is represented by exact
conditional quantiles and simulation, without a Normal approximation. The
translated model represents $p(y\mid c_S)$ and therefore omits the covariate-
density contribution to the joint FREM likelihood. Appendix A derives the
Gaussian nested case and both FFEM representations.

## Categorical covariates and parameter-dependent support

For an ordered categorical covariate $j$ with probabilities
$\pi_{j1},\ldots,\pi_{jK}$, category $k$ corresponds to the latent Gaussian
interval between cumulative-probability thresholds. Several observed
categories therefore contribute a joint multivariate-Normal rectangle mass.
The estimator avoids differentiating this rectangle by introducing
$V_{ij}\in(0,1)$ and

\[
 U_{ij}=b_{j,k-1}+V_{ij}\pi_{jk},\qquad
 b_{jk}=\sum_{r\leq k}\pi_{jr}.                           \tag{14}
\]

Integrating $V_{ij}$ recovers the category mass. This construction supports any
finite number of dependent binary, ordinal, or explicitly ordered nominal
covariates. A permutation-invariant nominal model instead requires a
multinomial latent-utility construction.

A regular continuous margin whose support depends on $\alpha_j$ uses the
analogous fixed-percentile representation

\[
 W_{ij}\in(0,1),\qquad
 X_{ij}=F_j^{-1}(W_{ij};\alpha_j).                         \tag{15}
\]

For a parameter coordinate with parameter-dependent support, the complete-data
score differentiates
$\phi_{ij}=(C_i\mu)_j+F_j^{-1}(W_{ij};\alpha_j)$ through
$\psi_i=h^{-1}(\phi_i)$ and the structural response. Missing covariates with
parameter-dependent support use the same representation.
Observed native values must remain in the interior of their support on the
visited parameter set; nonregular endpoint MLEs are outside the stationary-
interior theory.

## Experiments

The simulation study used four covariate-margin scenarios: Normal/Normal,
lognormal/Normal, Gamma/Normal, and Weibull/lognormal. Each contained 100
independently generated datasets with $N=100$, seven intravenous
one-compartment observations per subject, $V=10$, $CL=3$, and proportional
residual standard deviation 0.12. The four-dimensional Gaussian copula joined
two individual parameters and two covariates. Flexible families were
prespecified to isolate estimator behaviour from family selection. In the
coordinate order $(\eta_V,\eta_{CL},\mathrm{COV1},\mathrm{COV2})$, the six
generating Gaussian-score correlations were 0.25, 0.50, 0.10, 0.25, 0.55 and
0.20. COV1 was $N(70,14^2)$, lognormal with meanlog $\log(70)$ and sdlog 0.24,
Gamma with shape 7.5 and scale 12, or Weibull with shape 2.3 and scale 78.
COV2 was $N(90,25^2)$ in the first three scenarios and lognormal with meanlog
$\log(90)$ and sdlog 0.28 in the fourth. Each fit
used 1,500 score iterations, one persistent chain per subject, and two moves
from each of the three invariant kernels per iteration. The gain was
$0.2(k+30)^{-0.80}$, with score multiplier 0.025, $h_0=10^{-4}$ and 50
learning iterations. A Gaussian FREM fit supplied only a finite initializer;
all score-recursion state was restarted. For each dataset, the final score-SA
and Gaussian-FREM fits were reevaluated by importance sampling with 5,000 draws
and independent prespecified random-number seeds. A fit was considered
successful only if it completed, adaptation ended as specified, and no projection, invalid-step
backtracking, no-move replacement or one-sided numerical difference occurred
after adaptation.

Because Gamma shape and scale can compensate while retaining the marginal
mean, a separate direct-MLE experiment used 10,000 independently generated
Gamma samples at each of $N=50$, 100, 300, 1,000 and 3,000. Full-model Gamma
estimates were also compared with direct Gamma MLEs on the same $N=100$ and
$N=300$ datasets.

An additional example was used to evaluate prediction conditional on an
extreme covariate value. One dataset with $N=300$ was generated from the same
one-compartment model. C-reactive protein (CRP) followed a Gamma distribution
with shape 2 and scale 20, albumin followed $N(40,5^2)$, and the Gaussian-score
correlation between CRP and the clearance random effect was 0.55. Gaussian and
flexible-margin FREM were fitted with 1,500 iterations. An independent
validation population was then sampled above the 95th percentile of CRP. Only
CRP was supplied for prediction; albumin was integrated over its fitted
conditional distribution. Generating and fitted VPC quantiles were calculated
from 150,000 virtual subjects using common random numbers. Empirical validation
quantiles were calculated independently from 1,500 subjects. Predictive error
was the RMSE of log-transformed 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles over seven time
points.

# RESULTS

## Re-estimation study

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{Flexible-margin FREM parameter recovery and difference in estimated
joint observed-data log likelihood relative to Gaussian FREM. Bias is relative
mean bias across 100 datasets; $\Delta\ell$ is flexible-margin minus Gaussian
FREM.}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrrrr}
\toprule
Scenario & $V$ bias (\%) & $CL$ bias (\%) & Residual bias (\%) & $\Delta\ell$\\
\midrule
Normal/Normal       &  0.29 & -0.03 &  0.03 & -0.06\\
lognormal/Normal    & -0.03 & -0.46 & -0.15 &  4.30\\
Gamma/Normal        &  0.31 &  0.18 & -0.41 &  4.60\\
Weibull/lognormal   & -0.26 &  0.01 &  0.05 &  9.41\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Across scenarios, flexible-margin RMSE was 0.226--0.249 for $V$,
0.073--0.091 for $CL$, and 0.0033--0.0040 for residual standard deviation.
The corresponding Gaussian-FREM results were nearly identical: the largest
difference between methods in mean relative bias was 0.04 percentage points.

Estimates of the marginal-distribution parameters were close to their
generating values. Mean lognormal sdlog estimates were 0.239 and 0.277 for
generating values 0.240 and 0.280. Mean Weibull shape and scale estimates were
2.309 and 78.11 for generating values 2.3 and 78. Mean Gamma shape and scale
estimates were 7.944 and 11.556 for generating values 7.5 and 12. On the same
$N=100$ datasets, direct Gamma MLEs were 7.941 and 11.562; mean absolute
full-model--direct-MLE differences were 0.0065 and 0.0101. Thus the full model
reproduced the dataset-specific Gamma MLE. Across the six Gaussian-score
correlations, the maximum absolute scenario-specific mean bias was 0.022 and
RMSE ranged from 0.066 to 0.110.

The estimated joint observed-data log likelihood was larger for the flexible-
margin model in 285 of 300 datasets generated with a non-Gaussian margin:
90 lognormal/Normal, 95 Gamma/Normal and all 100 Weibull/lognormal datasets.
Under the Gaussian generating model, the mean difference was -0.06 and exactly
50 of 100 differences were positive, as expected for two numerical estimators
of the same model.

The covariate-density component accounted for mean log-likelihood differences
of 4.01, 4.15 and 8.58 in the lognormal/Normal, Gamma/Normal and
Weibull/lognormal scenarios. The corresponding mean differences in the
conditional response likelihood were 0.29, 0.45 and 0.83. Thus most of the
joint-likelihood gain arose from the specified covariate margins; the separate
predictive evaluation below addresses the effect on conditional prediction.

For each dataset, likelihoods were evaluated by independent importance-sampling
runs. The quadrature sum of the two reported Monte Carlo standard errors
averaged 0.29. The compared covariate margins had equal numbers of parameters,
but the models were non-nested; the reported differences are descriptive rather
than a formal model comparison. Equation (8a) further shows that a difference
in the joint log likelihood does not identify the corresponding difference in
$p(Y\mid c)$.

## Predictive evaluation

Both methods recovered the structural and residual-error parameters in the
additional example: estimates of $V$, $CL$ and residual standard deviation were
10.16, 3.01 and 0.120 for Gaussian FREM and 10.16, 3.00 and 0.120 for
flexible-margin FREM. The paired estimated joint log likelihood was -4091.6 and
-4041.7, respectively. Because the models are non-nested and the joint
likelihood includes the covariate density, this difference is descriptive.

The fitted conditional clearance relationships are shown in Figure 2. The
Gaussian-FREM relationship is the exact FFEM transformation implied by its
fitted Normal CRP margin and covariance matrix. It followed the centre of the
simulated data but increased too rapidly in the upper CRP tail. The flexible-
margin FREM transformation remained closer to the generating relationship.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.86\linewidth]{figures/figure2_conditional_relationship.png}
\caption{Conditional median clearance as a function of CRP in the simulated
$N=300$ dataset. Grey points are the true simulated individual clearance
values, which are latent rather than directly observed in an NLME analysis.
Lines show the generating conditional median and the relationships obtained
from Gaussian FREM and flexible-margin FREM after exact FFEM translation. Only
CRP is conditioned on; albumin is marginalized from the joint distribution.}
\end{figure}

In the independent high-CRP population, Gaussian FREM underestimated the lower
response percentile and overestimated the upper response percentile at later
times. The flexible-margin predictions were closer to the generating
percentiles throughout the profile. Log-scale VPC RMSE decreased from 0.266 to
0.123, a reduction of 53.9%. Albumin was not supplied for prediction and was
integrated out under both fitted joint distributions.

median and 10th/90th percentiles; black points show empirical quantiles in the
independent validation sample. Only CRP was available for prediction; albumin
was integrated out. Flexible-margin FREM reduced log-scale VPC RMSE from 0.266
to 0.123.}
\end{figure}

## Numerical verification

Independent numerical derivatives agreed with analytical complete-data scores
to $1.7\times10^{-10}$ for Gamma and Weibull examples and
$6.5\times10^{-8}$ for a lognormal example. Monte Carlo evaluations of
Fisher's identity included population parameters $\mu$, marginal parameters,
dependence parameters and residual error. With two categorical covariates, the
maximum absolute discrepancy was 0.0062, compared with a maximum Monte Carlo
standard error of 0.0113. For a parameter-dependent support example, the
maximum absolute discrepancy was $2.2\times10^{-10}$. Additional numerical
tests included multiple categorical covariates, centred Uniform and Gamma
parameter random effects, and missing Uniform covariates.

In the direct Gamma-MLE experiment, mean shape bias decreased from 2.83% at
$N=100$ to 0.14% at $N=3,000$, and mean scale bias decreased from -0.85% to
-0.07%; bias in their product remained within 0.05%. Mean absolute
full-model--direct-MLE differences in shape and scale were 0.0043 and 0.0075
in the $N=300$ datasets. These results show that the shape--scale displacement
in the $N=100$ re-estimation study reflected finite-sample Gamma-MLE behaviour
and simulation-replicate variation rather than score-recursion error.

For Normal parameter and covariate margins, exported raw-scale coefficients and
UPV covariance agreed with the direct FREM block formulas to less than
$10^{-12}$. With a Gamma covariate and Normal parameter margins, 100,000 draws
from the translated FFEM reproduced its analytical conditional means within
0.003 and covariance elements within 0.002. With a centred Gamma parameter
margin, analytical conditional quantiles agreed with 150,000 exact conditional
draws within 0.006. In the fitted CRP example, direct copula-FREM and translated
FFEM conditional densities were identical to numerical precision, and the
translated and direct concentration predictions were identical for every
tested draw.

# DISCUSSION

The proposed extension replaces the multivariate Normal population
distribution of FREM by a Gaussian-copula distribution with prespecified
margins; the structural and residual-error models are unchanged. When all
margins are Normal, the two population distributions coincide. In the
non-Gaussian simulation scenarios, the flexible-margin model gave larger
estimated joint log likelihoods while structural-parameter biases remained
small for both approaches. The principal difference was observed in prediction
conditional on covariate-tail values. A misspecified marginal CDF changes the
Gaussian score assigned to a covariate value and therefore changes the fitted
conditional distribution $p(\eta_{\mathrm{par}}\mid c)$, even when the first two
moments are estimated accurately.

The conditional representation provides an explicit covariate model for a
chosen subset. With Normal parameter margins it is a conventional FFEM using
fixed transformed covariates. With non-Normal parameter margins it retains the
fitted distribution through a latent-Normal quantile transformation. Direct
copula-FREM and translated-model predictions are identical when the fitted
population parameters are held fixed. Re-estimation of the translated model
instead targets $p(y\mid c_S)$ and does not include the covariate-density term
from the joint FREM likelihood.

The lack of a general finite sufficient statistic changes the stochastic-
approximation step but not the likelihood being estimated. Population
parameters were updated with the controlled-Markov stochastic-gradient
algorithm described by Delyon et al. Fisher's identity shows that its mean
field equals the gradient of the specified observed-data log likelihood. The
convergence result is conditional on the stated stability, drift, regularity
and critical-value assumptions. The reported numerical diagnostics establish
that the finite-run stabilization criteria were satisfied, but do not
establish these asymptotic assumptions.

Model-based copulas have previously been used in pharmacometrics to generate
virtual populations from covariate distributions [@guo2024]. The present
extension concerns likelihood-based estimation of the joint parameter-
covariate distribution within a nonlinear mixed-effects model.

The simulation is exploratory: one PK model, 100 datasets per scenario,
prespecified families and a Gaussian finite initializer were used. Coverage,
observed-information standard errors, cold-start sensitivity, automatic family
learning and powered categorical or moving-support studies remain future work.
General non-Gaussian R-vines require additional score calculations and are
outside the fixed Gaussian-copula scope. The continuous margins considered here
must be proper, differentiable and identifiable with finite score moments on
the stabilized compact set; parameter random-effect margins are centred and
require finite variance. These conditions include many non-Gaussian families
but do not define a distribution-free estimator. Nonregular
support-boundary MLEs and permutation-invariant nominal variables also require
separate theory. The current implementation also requires every estimated
structural parameter to belong to the population-location block; estimated
fixed-only structural parameters are outside its scope.

# CONCLUSION

Flexible-margin Gaussian-copula FREM separates the specification of marginal
distributions from the specification of dependence and reduces to Gaussian
FREM when all margins are Normal. Fisher's identity links the mean field of the
controlled-MCMC stochastic-gradient algorithm to the observed-data likelihood
score. In the simulations considered here, structural-parameter recovery was
similar under both approaches, whereas flexible margins provided larger
estimated joint log likelihoods and more accurate prediction conditional on
extreme covariate values under non-Gaussian data-generating distributions. The
fitted conditional model can be exported without loss to a conventional FFEM
when parameter margins are Normal and to the exact conditional generative
representation otherwise.

# Likelihood normalization, Fisher identity and FFEM translation

## Continuous normalization

For fixed $\theta$, the map $x_j\mapsto \xi_j=\Phi^{-1}\{F_j(x_j)\}$ has
Jacobian $d\xi_j/dx_j=f_j(x_j)/\phi(\xi_j)$. Substitution in (7) therefore gives

\[
 p_{\theta_p}(x)\,dx
 =\phi_R(\xi)\,d\xi.
\]

Integration over $\R^d$ is one. This proves normalization for any proper
absolutely continuous margins; Gaussian marginal shape is not required.

## Several categorical covariates

For observed category vector $k_{\mathcal D}$, let
$u_j=b_{j,k_j-1}+v_j\pi_{j,k_j}$ for $j\in\mathcal D$. The augmented mixed
density is

\[
 p_\theta^{\rm aug}(x_{\mathcal C},k_{\mathcal D},v_{\mathcal D})
 =c_R(u)\prod_{j\in\mathcal C}f_j(x_j)
   \prod_{j\in\mathcal D}\pi_{j,k_j}.                     \tag{A1}
\]

Since $du_j=\pi_{j,k_j}dv_j$, integrating
$v_{\mathcal D}\in(0,1)^{|\mathcal D|}$ gives the Gaussian-copula rectangle
mass for $k_{\mathcal D}$. Summing category vectors tiles the latent unit cube,
so the masses sum to one. Missing categories add counting-measure summation and
remain normalized.

## Moving continuous support

For $X=F_\alpha^{-1}(W)$ with $W\in(0,1)$,
$dW=f_\alpha(X)dX$. Thus a latent moving-support coordinate contributes the
fixed reference $dW$ and its marginal density factor disappears after change
of variables. Dependence still enters through
$\xi=\Phi^{-1}(W)$. If the coordinate affects the response,
$p_{\theta}\{Y\mid h^{-1}(C\mu+F_\alpha^{-1}(W))\}$ is differentiated
through both $\mu$ and $F_\alpha^{-1}$. The moving-boundary derivative is therefore represented by the
pathwise quantile derivative rather than discarded.

## Observed likelihood and Fisher identity

Multiplying the normalized population density by the conditional response
density and integrating over all unobserved coordinates gives $g_i(\theta)$. Under
an integrable derivative envelope,

\[
\begin{aligned}
E_\vartheta[\nabla\log \widetilde f_i(Z_i;\vartheta)\mid O_i]
&=\int \frac{\nabla \widetilde f_i(z;\vartheta)}
                  {\widetilde f_i(z;\vartheta)}
       \frac{\widetilde f_i(z;\vartheta)}
            {\widetilde g_i(\vartheta)}\,\lambda(dz)\\
&=\frac{\nabla\int \widetilde f_i(z;\vartheta)\lambda(dz)}
        {\widetilde g_i(\vartheta)}
 =\nabla\log \widetilde g_i(\vartheta).
\end{aligned}
\]

The chain rule gives
$\nabla_\vartheta\bar\ell=J_\tau(\vartheta)^{\mathsf T}
\nabla_\theta\bar\ell$. A nonsingular $J_\tau$ makes native- and internal-
coordinate stationary points equivalent.

## Gaussian nested model and FFEM translation

When every margin is Normal, write $X=\mu+D\xi$, where
$\xi\sim N_d(0,R)$ and $D$ is the diagonal matrix of marginal standard
deviations. It follows directly that

\[
 X\sim N_d(\mu,DRD).                                      \tag{A2}
\]

Thus the all-Normal Gaussian-copula model is the standard multivariate-Normal
FREM model with $\Omega_{\mathrm{FREM}}=DRD$; it is not an approximation to
that model.

Let $P$ index the parameter random effects and let $S$ be any selected subset
of continuous covariates. Marginalizing covariates outside $S$ leaves the
Gaussian subvector $(\xi_P,\xi_S)$ with the corresponding submatrix of $R$.
The multivariate-Normal conditioning formula gives

\[
 \xi_P\mid \xi_S=z_S
 =B_{\xi,S}z_S+L_S\varepsilon,
 \qquad
 B_{\xi,S}=R_{P,S}R_{S,S}^{-1},
 \qquad
 L_SL_S^{\mathsf T}
 =R_{P,P}-B_{\xi,S}R_{S,P},                              \tag{A3}
\]

where $\varepsilon\sim N(0,I)$. If the parameter margins are Normal,
$\eta_P=D_P\xi_P$; substitution in (A3) yields the coefficient matrix
$D_PB_{\xi,S}$ and UPV covariance
$D_PL_SL_S^{\mathsf T}D_P$ stated in the conventional FFEM representation.
If the selected covariate margins are also Normal, replacing
$z_S$ by $D_S^{-1}(c_S-\mu_S)$ gives the usual raw-scale FREM coefficient
matrix and Schur-complement UPV covariance.

For continuous non-Normal parameter margins, let $Q_\eta$ apply their quantile
functions componentwise. Since
$\eta_P=Q_\eta\{\Phi(\xi_P)\}$, (A3) gives

\[
 \eta_P\mid c_S
 =Q_\eta\!\left[\Phi\!\left\{
 B_{\xi,S}z_S(c_S)+L_S\varepsilon\right\}\right].        \tag{A4}
\]

Equation (A4) is the distributional FFEM representation in the main text and
has exactly the same conditional law as the fitted FREM. For an ordered
categorical covariate, conditioning is instead on its latent Gaussian interval;
integrating (A3) over the corresponding truncated-Normal score distribution
gives the stated interval mixture. Finally, direct FREM and translated-FFEM
predictions integrate the same response kernel $p(Y\mid\eta_P)$ against this
same conditional distribution. Their conditional predictive distributions are
therefore identical when the population parameters are held fixed.

# Controlled kernel and convergence details

## Exact conditional-population proposal

Let $q_{\vartheta,i}(\psi)$ denote the population density of $\psi_i$
conditional on observed covariates, from which proposals are sampled exactly,
and let
$L_{\vartheta,i}(\psi)=p_{\theta}(Y_i\mid\psi,x_i)$. Then

\[
 \pi_{\vartheta,i}(\psi)=
 \frac{L_{\vartheta,i}(\psi)q_{\vartheta,i}(\psi)}
      {\int L_{\vartheta,i}(v)q_{\vartheta,i}(v)dv}.
\]

Suppose uniformly on the compact parameter set that
$L_{\vartheta,i}(\psi)\leq M_i$ and its normalizer is at least $m_i>0$.
The independence-Metropolis weight
$w=\pi/q$ is bounded by $M_i/m_i$, and therefore

\[
 P^{\rm ind}_{\vartheta,i}(\psi,A)
 \geq(m_i/M_i)\Pi_{\vartheta,i}(A).                        \tag{B1}
\]

Composition with any other invariant Metropolis kernels preserves the
minorization. With finitely many subjects and chains, the product chain has a
uniform Doeblin bound. Exact conditional augmentation after the eta move also
preserves it: if $R_\vartheta(da\mid\psi')$ draws missing/categorical/fixed-
reference variables, then

\[
 \widetilde P_\vartheta\{(\psi,a),d\psi' da'\}
 =P_\vartheta(\psi,d\psi')R_\vartheta(da'\mid\psi')
 \geq\epsilon\Pi_\vartheta(d\psi',da').                   \tag{B2}
\]

If a rejection sampler for a multivariate category rectangle reaches its
finite iteration limit, the iteration is terminated without substituting an
approximate draw.

## Markovian stochastic-approximation decomposition

After finite adaptation, write the score noise as the conditional mean plus a
martingale term, a Poisson-equation remainder and numerical error:

\[
 \widehat H_{k+1}=\nabla\bar\ell(\vartheta_k)
  +e_{k+1}+r^{\rm P}_{k+1}+r^{\rm num}_{k+1}.              \tag{B3}
\]

Here is the precise mapping to Fort et al. [@fort2016]. On every visited
compact parameter set, assume their H1--H2 with a drift function $W$: the
partially marginalized score is uniformly $W$-bounded, each
$P_\vartheta$ has unique invariant distribution $\Pi_\vartheta$, the kernels
are uniformly $W$-geometrically ergodic, and, for some $p\geq2$,

\[
 \sup_\vartheta P_\vartheta W^p\leq\rho W^p+b,
 \qquad \rho<1.                                           \tag{B4}
\]

The common minorization in (B1)--(B2), together with Lipschitz dependence of
the kernel after finite adaptation, supplies H3 with exponent $\upsilon=1$. H4 is the following
integrated local-oscillation condition for the actual fixed-preconditioner
increment $\mathcal H_\vartheta$: for every compact $K$ and $\delta>0$,

\[
 \sup_{\vartheta\in K}\int\Pi_\vartheta(dx)
 \sup_{\substack{\vartheta'\in K\\
                  \|\vartheta'-\vartheta\|\leq\delta}}
 \|\mathcal H_{\vartheta'}(x)-\mathcal H_\vartheta(x)\|
 \leq C_K\delta^\alpha,\qquad \alpha=1.                 \tag{B5}
\]

Smoothness of the mean field alone does not imply (B5); it is a stated
regularity condition. Under H1--H4, the associated Poisson-equation solutions
have the bounds used by Fort et al. Proposition 4.11. Their H6 requires a
power-law gain exponent satisfying

\[
 a>\max\!\left\{\frac1p,
 \frac{1+(\alpha\wedge\upsilon)/p}
      {1+(\alpha\wedge\upsilon)}\right\}.                \tag{B6}
\]

For $p\geq2$ and $\alpha=\upsilon=1$, the implemented $a=0.80>0.75$
satisfies (B6), not merely the usual Robbins--Monro sums.

After safeguards become inactive, apply Fort et al. Proposition 4.6 to the
stopped tail recursion with mean field $h=A\nabla\bar\ell$. Its C-i follows
from differentiability, C-ii from compact-tail stability, and C-iii from the
gain. For H5 and C-v(A), assume a coercive continuously differentiable
extension $w$ that equals $-\bar\ell+C$ near the visited compact tail, has
compact level sets and compact zero-drift set

\[
 \mathcal L_w=\{\vartheta:
   \langle\nabla w(\vartheta),h(\vartheta)\rangle=0\},
\]

such that $w(\mathcal L_w)$ has empty interior and
$\mathcal L_w\cap K_{\rm tail}=\mathcal L\cap K_{\rm tail}$. This global
extension and its critical-value property are assumptions, not automatic
consequences of local likelihood smoothness.

It remains to establish Proposition 4.6 C-iv. Apply Fort et al. Proposition
4.11 and Corollary 4.12 to the process stopped on exit from the compact tail;
eventual safeguard inactivity makes the exit time infinite from some finite
random time onward. For its weighted controlled-Markov perturbation $\xi_j$,
write

\[
 A_k=\sup_{l\geq k}\left\|\sum_{j=k}^l\gamma_j\xi_j\right\|.
\]

Overlapping partial sums give $A_n\leq2A_k$ whenever $n\geq k$. Hence, for
every $\delta>0$,

\[
 \{\limsup_n A_n\geq\delta\}
 \subseteq\bigcap_k\{A_k\geq\delta/2\}.                 \tag{B7}
\]

Corollary 4.12 gives
$P(A_k\geq\delta/2)\to0$, so the probability of the intersection is zero.
A countable sequence of positive rational $\delta$ proves $A_k\to0$ almost
surely on the no-exit tail. Thus C-iv holds. Proposition 4.6 then yields
$d(\vartheta_k,\mathcal L)\to0$ almost surely. The finite prefix cannot change
the limit set. This is a conditional stationary-set result for Delyon et al.'s
stochastic-gradient equation (74), not an invocation of their finite-statistic
SAEM Theorem 5 or 8.

# Numerical score error

For centered differences, suppose

\[
 \mathcal H_{h_k}(\vartheta,u)=\mathcal H(\vartheta,u)+r_k(\vartheta,u),
 \qquad \|r_k(\vartheta,u)\|\leq h_k^2M(u),
\]

with $\sup_kE\{M(Z_k)\}<\infty$. Taking $h_k=h_0\sqrt{\gamma_k}$,
Tonelli's theorem gives

\[
 E\!\left[\sum_k \gamma_k\|r_k\|\right]
 \leq C\sum_k \gamma_kh_k^2
 =Ch_0^2\sum_k \gamma_k^2<\infty.                         \tag{C1}
\]

The nonnegative random series is therefore finite almost surely. This controls
the complete random numerical perturbation, not merely its conditional mean.
Post-freeze one-sided differences are rejected because they do not satisfy the
same centered second-order error statement.

The reported endpoint averages internal-coordinate iterates after finite burn-
in. If raw iterates converge to an isolated stationary point, their Cesaro
average has the same limit. No asymptotic-efficiency claim for the average is
made; Markov-chain trajectory averaging requires additional assumptions
[@liang2010].
